title: Wisdom
hookLine: the fourth perfection: seeing clearly, before the questions pile up
tomorrow: how do you tell the top of a stick from its root?

lines: THE GROUP CHAT FILLS UP FAST.
A MAN WITH AN ARROW IN HIS SIDE.
cards: Something goes wrong for a friend, and the group chat fills up fast: whose fault it was, what it means, what everyone else would have done. Nobody has asked what she needs right now.
A monk named Malunkyaputta brings the Buddha that same pattern, in a story from the Middle Length Discourses. He arrives with an ultimatum. Is the world eternal or not?
Does an awakened one exist after death? Answer these, he says, or I quit the monk's life. The Buddha doesn't give him the answers.
He gives him a man with an arrow in his side.

teach.b: The arrow is smeared thick with poison. His friends bring a surgeon. And the wounded man says: wait.
Nobody pulls this out until I know who shot me. His name and clan. Tall or short.
What village he's from. What the bow was made of, the string, the feathers. The man would die, the Buddha says, before any of it was known.
It's not that the questions are silly. It's that they aren't what is happening. What is happening is a wound.
Here is the fourth perfection: panna, wisdom. In these texts it isn't knowing a lot. It's seeing what is actually in front of you, as it is.
The Buddha says plainly what he did teach instead: suffering, where it comes from, its ending, and the path to its ending, because that is what helps.
And the wounded man isn't a fool. He's frightened, and fear wants explanations. Wisdom here looks almost plain.
The who and the why can come later, if they matter at all.

how: In Theravada teaching, wisdom (panna) is the fourth of the ten perfections; Buddhists cultivate it through study, reflection and meditation, and the arrow parable is often retold in talks about what to set aside.

o: a large store of facts about the universe
seeing clearly what is actually happening
a calm mood that comes from meditating

games.q: inside the arrow story — tap the pairs.
p: no surgeon till he knows who shot

s: in Buddhist texts, wisdom means knowing as much as possible
panna is seeing what is actually here. the man with the arrow wanted more facts, and would have died waiting.
the Buddha answered Malunkyaputta's questions about the universe
he left them unanswered and told the arrow story instead.
wisdom comes after giving, virtue and renunciation in the list of perfections
it's the fourth of the ten.

games.q: your friend's laptop dies the night before her paper is due. she starts listing everyone who told her to back up her files. what would the arrow story say?
o: first: is the file saved anywhere? the blame can wait.
first: work out exactly why the laptop crashed.
first: agree with her that it's not her fault.
games.why: the wounded man wanted the archer's name before the surgeon. the arrow comes first; the why can wait.

practice: Bring one problem to mind, something live this week. Notice the arrow questions you've been asking, why me, whose fault, and set them down for now.
Then name, in a few plain words, only what is actually happening, and the first useful step.

wordCard.voice: Panna: wisdom, the fourth of the ten perfections. Not knowing more, but seeing what is actually here.

orig.note: Pali: wisdom, seeing things as they are. Sanskrit prajna.

carryVoice: Keep this one: see clearly, the arrow first and the questions after, if they matter at all. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: MN 63, Culamalunkya Sutta (the questions set aside; the man wounded by a poisoned arrow; what the Buddha did teach)
The ten perfections (dasa parami): Buddhavamsa; Jataka Nidanakatha
